title: Charged with grandeur
hookLine: Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God

cards: Hold a sheet of kitchen foil near a window and give it a shake. For a split second it throws light everywhere, then goes dull again.
Gerard Manley Hopkins used that exact picture, shaken foil, in a short poem about God and the world.

He was a Christian poet and a Jesuit priest, and his poem names God in its first line and the Holy Ghost in its closing lines. Between them, he says the world is like that foil. Shake it, and it flashes.

teach.b: The poem is God's Grandeur, and it opens: "The world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil". First, charged.
A charged thing is loaded, ready to go off, like a storm cloud before lightning. Hopkins doesn't say grandeur sits in the world quietly. It's packed in, waiting to break out.
Second, two ways it breaks out. It flames out, sudden, like the foil.
And it "gathers to a greatness, like the ooze of oil crushed": slow and heavy, the way oil seeps from something pressed. Third, the honest middle.
Hopkins doesn't pretend the world is all shining: "Generations have trod, have trod, have trod; and all is seared with trade; bleared, smeared with toil".
The soil is bare, and feet in shoes, he says, can't even feel it anymore.
Fourth, the turn: "And for all this, nature is never spent; there lives the dearest freshness deep down things". Not on the surface. Deep down.
The poem closes with its reason: "Because the Holy Ghost over the bent world broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings."
For Hopkins the freshness has a source, and he names it in the language of his Christian faith.
Some readers who don't share that faith still come back to the first two images: a world that flashes, and a world that seeps.

how: Christians who love poetry often read God's Grandeur as a prayer of praise, and people on a personal spiritual path use its images of shaken foil and deep-down freshness as a prompt for noticing beauty in worn, everyday places.

games.q: you've just written that the world is charged with God's grandeur. then you look at ground worn down by generations of work and trade. what do you write next?
o: say the wear plainly, then say freshness lives deep down.
games.why: Hopkins names the wear ("seared with trade") and then turns: "for all this, nature is never spent."

practice: Look slowly around for anything that catches the light, a glass, a leaf, a drop of water, someone's hair, and when you find it, watch how the light moves as you move your head a little.
If nothing flashes, look for the slow kind instead, something quietly lovely that's been there all along. If you pray, you can let the poem's first line be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: shook foil. Hopkins's image, from God's Grandeur, for the world's grandeur flashing out all at once, like sudden light. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: charged. Even on worn, trodden ground, a freshness lives deep down. Until tomorrow.
